notes:
I've gathered substantial material from multiple sources. Here are my verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Ecclesiastes 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "There is another evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily upon mankind"

**Traditional Reading:** The Preacher (Solomon) introduces a specific case-study of an "evil" (or "tragedy") he has observed. He still speaks from his "under the sun" premise — life viewed from a purely earthly, God-absent perspective. The Hebrew suggests this evil is "heavy" or "great" upon humanity, not merely common. Ellicott notes the phrase should be translated "heavy upon" rather than "common among." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Gill identifies this evil specifically as covetousness — a man who hoards wealth without enjoying it — and notes it was widespread even in Solomon's day when silver was as common as stones in Jerusalem. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Precept Austin (William Barrick) notes this introduces "Case History #1: A Full Treasury" — Solomon demonstrating that prosperity is not always as good as it appears. The formula "There is" introduces specific examples for argumentation throughout Ecclesiastes. "Under the sun" signals the viewpoint: mere mortal beings conducting their lives without God face enigmas seemingly without solution. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

---

### v. 2: "God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor… yet God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them."

**Traditional Reading:** The tragic paradox: a man has every external blessing — riches, wealth, honor, all his heart desires — yet God withholds the ability to enjoy them. Having is not the same as enjoying. David Guzik (Enduring Word) calls it "possession without participation." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Ellicott observes that "riches, wealth, and honour" are the three words used together regarding Solomon himself in 2 Chronicles 1:11. This may be autobiographical — Solomon speaking of his own experience and perhaps thinking of Jeroboam as the "foreigner" who would consume his kingdom's wealth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Gill explains that the "power to eat" means not merely appetite but the heart to enjoy what one has. He notes the "stranger" may be an unrelated person who, by lawful or unlawful means, comes into possession of everything. He quotes Juvenal: it is "frenzy and madness for a man to live poor, that he may die rich." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Precept Austin adds: "God alone controls both the giving and the enjoying." Charles Swindoll connects this to Solomon personally: Solomon received "riches and wealth and honor" from God, yet as his reign progressed and he drifted from God, the enjoyment was lost. Matthew Henry is quoted: "Because he has not the will to serve God with it, God denies him the power to serve himself with it." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

---

### v. 3: "A man may father a hundred children and live for many years… if he is unsatisfied… I say that a stillborn child is better off than he."

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon uses hyperbole (a hundred children, extreme longevity) to make a profound point. In ancient Israel, many children were the supreme sign of blessing (Psalm 127:3–5) and long life was considered divine favor. Yet if the soul is not satisfied with goodness and the man receives no proper burial, a stillborn child is better off. "To die unburied was the mark of a despised and unmourned end. Better to miscarry at birth than to miscarry throughout life" (Eaton, cited by Guzik). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Ellicott notes that while failure to enjoy riches is common, lacking a burial is not necessarily so — suggesting the Preacher may have had a specific actual occurrence in mind. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Gill expands: this man "has no burial" meaning he is either destroyed by robbers for his wealth, or is so sordid he refuses to provide for his own decent burial, or his heirs neglect him. The stillborn child is preferred because it never experienced the crushing disappointment of meaninglessness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Precept Austin (Bible.org) notes this seems to contradict traditional wisdom teachings — that children and long life guarantee blessing. Life without God is not authentic life, regardless of external signs. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

---

### v. 4: "For a stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity."

**Traditional Reading:** The "he" (KJV) should be translated "it" — referring to the stillborn child (Ellicott). The child comes into the world in vain, never answers any purpose, departs into the darkness of the grave unnoticed, and has no name remembered. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Gill notes that though the stillborn's circumstances are tragic and obscure, in this respect it has the advantage over the covetous rich man: "though he is covered with darkness, yet no ill is ever spoken of him; whereas the name of the wicked covetous man is cursed." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Precept Austin lists six characteristics of the stillborn from the text: its birth is in vain, it goes into obscurity, its name is covered in darkness, it never sees the sun, it never has wisdom, yet — shockingly — it is better off. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

---

### v. 5: "The child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man"

**Traditional Reading:** The stillborn has never seen the light of the sun, never experienced its comfort, never known anything — neither good nor evil, neither pleasure nor pain. Gill notes the Targum adds: "the light of the law he seeth not; and knoweth not between good and evil." Because it has never known the troubles of life, it has more rest than the unsatisfied rich man. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Guzik: "In Solomon's mind, the stillborn child — tragic as it is — is better off than the man who knows the crushing disappointment of the realization of meaninglessness." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

---

### v. 6: "even if he lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. Do not all go to the same place?"

**Traditional Reading:** Even a lifespan of two thousand years (hyperbole — Methuselah lived only 969 years) means nothing without enjoyment of good. "Do not all go to one place?" refers to Sheol, the grave — the common fate of all. Both the stillborn and the rich man, the satisfied and unsatisfied, all go to the same place. From an "under the sun" perspective, death is the great equalizer that cancels all apparent advantages. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Gill notes some interpreted "one place" as hell where all sinners go, but he favors the grave interpretation. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Ellicott observes the unusual Hebrew conjunction "though" is found elsewhere only in Esther 7:4. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

---

### v. 7: "All a man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied."

**Traditional Reading:** Man works to feed his body, but the deeper appetite (Hebrew *nephesh* = "soul") is never filled by physical consumption. Precept Austin emphasizes the Hebrew word for "appetite" is *nephesh*, translated "soul" over 200 times in the OT — indicating this is about spiritual dissatisfaction, not just physical hunger. Food, money, or comfort may sustain you temporarily but cannot fill the eternal longing of the heart. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

Guzik notes Solomon anticipated what Moses and Jesus both taught: "Man does not live by bread alone" (Deuteronomy 8:3, Matthew 4:4). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Gill: "the mind of man grasps after greater things, and can find no contentment or satisfaction in earthly or sensual enjoyments." Labor is for the body only; it cannot reach the soul. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

---

### v. 8: "What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool? What gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others?"

**Traditional Reading:** In the face of death and the inability of wealth to satisfy, wisdom offers no real advantage. Both the wise and the fool get hungry; both face the same diseases and death. Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: "The necessaries of life are the same to both, and their condition in life is nearly similar; liable to the same diseases, dissolution, and death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Gill offers two interpretations: either the poor man who is diligent and knows how to live among men enjoys as much as the rich man; or the poor man with understanding has no more advantage than the poor fool who merely has enough sense to get bread. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Ellicott: "That knoweth to walk — Understands how to conduct himself. But why this should be limited to the poor is not obvious." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Pett's Commentary: "In the face of these vicissitudes of life, and especially in the face of death… what advantage does the wise man have over the fool?… Illness and death are the great equalisers for all." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ecclesiastes-6.html)

---

### v. 9: "Better what the eye can see than the wandering of the desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind."

**Traditional Reading:** It is better to enjoy what one actually possesses (what the eye can see) than to let the soul roam in endless, unsatisfied craving (the wandering of desire). Gill explains: "It is better to enjoy contentedly things in sight and in possession, than to let the mind loose in vague desires, after things that may never be come at, and, if attained to, would give no satisfaction." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Guzik: "The Preacher knew that in a world of such uncertainty and absence of meaning, what one can actually see is always better than what one merely desires." This is the last of nine occurrences of "striving after wind" in Ecclesiastes, closing the section on the futility of human achievement (1:12–6:9). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

---

### v. 10: "Whatever exists was named long ago, and what happens to a man is foreknown; but he cannot contend with one stronger than he."

**Traditional Reading:** This is one of the more difficult verses. Ellicott translates: "What he is his name has been called long ago, and it is known that it is man; neither may he strive" — meaning the name given to man long ago (Adam, from *adamah*, the earth — Genesis 2:7) indicates his weakness and creatureliness. He cannot contend with the Almighty. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Gill sees three layers: (1) all things are determined and appointed by God in His eternal decrees; (2) all men, even the most famous, are merely "man" — weak, frail, mortal; (3) therefore man should not contend with God who is mightier. He notes that the Masorites observed this verse is the exact middle of the book of Ecclesiastes. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Guzik calls this "a fatalistic view of God's sovereignty" — God is completely in control, and man is too weak to resist. "Many today refuse to know what the Preacher knew. They believe that when they face God they will in fact contend with Him, and tell God a thing or two. Such are seriously and sadly deluded." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

---

### v. 11: "For the more words, the more futility — and how does that profit anyone?"

**Traditional Reading:** Human disputation, whether with God or with one another, cannot solve the problem of meaningless life. Ellicott notes the word can be translated either "things" or "words" — both make sense: many words increase vanity (arguments and complaints against God are futile), or many things (possessions) increase vanity (the more one possesses, the more acutely one feels the emptiness). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "Evidently the thought of the preacher is that the more a man possesses under the sun, the more profoundly conscious does he become of the vanity and vexation of it all." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Gill prefers "things" — wisdom, wealth, pleasure, power all increase vanity; man is no better for any of them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

---

### v. 12: "For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?"

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter ends on a note of ignorance and uncertainty — entirely appropriate to the "under the sun" perspective. No one truly knows what is good for a person in this brief, shadow-like life. Gill: "since therefore he has so short a time to enjoy anything in, it is hard to say what is best for him to have, and the rather since he is quite ignorant of what is to come." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

Guzik observes: "We often think we know what is good for us; but do we really? In the course of a life, which is better: Wealth or poverty? Health or sickness? Fame or obscurity? Many who have what is commonly thought of as good are not the better for it." The chapter "winds its way down to a depressing and uncertain finish, well suited to the state of man on his own" (Kidner). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

Guzik adds a crucial theological note: Solomon's lack of knowledge about the afterlife reflects Old Testament limitations — "Jesus Christ brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (2 Timothy 1:10). The understanding of the afterlife was cloudy in the Old Testament; the New Testament provides clarity about heaven, hell, and judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

---

## Protestant Traditions — Points of Difference

### Reformed / Baptist (John Piper, Desiring God)
Piper expounds Ecclesiastes 6:1–2 by stressing God's sovereignty over *both* the giving of possessions and the power to enjoy them. In his article "When Enjoying Money and Possessions Is a Work of Grace," he argues that "all truly God-honoring delight in creation is a miraculous gift of God" — none of us produces this delight from our fallen selves. The purpose of pointing out these "grievous evils" is "to make us despair that meaning and joy can finally be found in this world under the sun." The lesson: "Don't set your heart on riches." Piper connects this directly to 1 Timothy 6:17–18 and the call to take hold of "that which is truly life." (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/when-enjoying-money-and-possessions-is-a-work-of-grace)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word)
Guzik reads the chapter through the lens of the "under the sun" premise — life viewed without God. His emphasis is pastoral and application-oriented: the chapter exposes the emptiness of wealth, the tragedy of dissatisfaction, and the powerlessness of man before God. He stresses that we have a clear New Testament hope about the afterlife that Solomon lacked. He also quotes Eaton: "Like the Mosaic law (cf. Galatians 3:22), the Preacher is slamming every door except the door of faith." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-6/)

### Anglican (Charles Ellicott)
Ellicott's commentary focuses on textual and philological details: translation choices ("heavy upon" vs "common among"), the unusual conjunction in v. 6 found only in Esther, the Chaldee word for "mightier" in v. 10 used only in later Hebrew, the possible reference to Genesis 2:7 and 6:3. He reads v. 10 as about the name "man" (*Adam*) indicating weakness. His approach is scholarly and restrained, typical of 19th-century Anglican commentary. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

### Baptist (John Gill, 18th century)
Gill interprets the entire chapter primarily as an exposé of covetousness. He sees the "evil" of v. 1 as specifically the sin of covetousness — "one of the evil things that come out of the heart of man… the root of all evil." He reads v. 10 christologically in passing (mentioning "the second man, the Lord from heaven") but ultimately favors the interpretation that all men are merely "man," weak and mortal. His approach weaves together Scripture cross-references, rabbinic sources (Jarchi), and classical quotations (Juvenal). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/6.htm)

### Evangelical (Precept Austin / Bible.org)
Precept Austin compiles insights from multiple evangelical commentators (William Barrick, Warren Wiersbe, Charles Swindoll, Ray Pritchard, F.B. Meyer). The emphasis is on the paradox that God gives both the blessing and the power to enjoy it — and can withhold either. Life "under the sun" (without God) cannot yield satisfaction. The site draws practical application: "Only the Lord can enable the soul to taste the goodness in what He provides." It also includes devotional reflections (e.g., Watchman Nee's illustration of full hands unable to take God's hand). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship
I was unable to access bibleodyssey.org or the NET Bible notes directly due to tool limitations. However, Precept Austin cites William P. Brown (Interpretation commentary, 2000): "Ownership is, thus, a misnomer. One's possessions are exclusively gifts of God, and as easily as God gives, so God takes away to give to others. The givenness of material possessions is a two-edged sword." This reflects a modern scholarly emphasis on the theological destabilizing of human ownership. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings
I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary on Ecclesiastes 6. These sources were not reached in my searches.

### Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace
No content from these traditions regarding Ecclesiastes 6 was found in the accessible sources. However, Precept Austin directly counters prosperity-thinking: "Ecclesiastes 6:2 shows us that having is not the same as enjoying… This is the danger of thinking success equals satisfaction. It doesn't." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-6-commentary)
